source_refs.note: Book p. 275: heading 14.3 Cross Product or Vector Product; no text printed before 14.3.1, so the page is our overview of the section.

blocks.text: In the book, the heading 14.3 Cross Product or Vector Product is followed at once by its first sub-heading, 14.3.1; nothing else is printed under the main heading. The notes below are our own overview of the section.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In 14.2 we multiplied two vectors with the dot product and got a scalar (a plain number). In 14.3 we learn the second way of multiplying two vectors: the cross product \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).
Its answer is a vector, and that vector is perpendicular to both \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\). This is why it is also called the vector product.
The cross product is defined only for vectors in space (three dimensions): a direction perpendicular to two vectors needs a third dimension.

rows: Zero when the vectors are perpendicular
Zero vector when the vectors are parallel
Used for angles, projection, work done
Used for perpendicular vectors, areas, moment of a force
blocks.caption: Dot product compared with cross product (our summary)

blocks.text: What this section covers, sub-heading by sub-heading:

items: 14.3.1 The definition \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = (|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta)\,\underline{n}\) and the right hand rule for the direction.
14.3.2 Parallel vectors: their cross product is \(\underline{0}\).
14.3.3 Cross products of \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) and the result \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\).
14.3.5 The determinant formula for \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) in components (Example 15).
14.3.6 The sine of the angle between two vectors (Examples 16-19).
14.3.7 Applications: area of a parallelogram and of a triangle, moment of a force (Examples 20-22).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
Before you start, revise two things:
1. Unit vectors \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) along the \(x\)-, \(y\)- and \(z\)-axes, and the magnitude \(|a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}| = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}\).
2. Expanding a \(3 \times 3\) determinant along the first row: \(\begin{vmatrix} p & q & r \\ a & b & c \\ d & e & f \end{vmatrix} = p(bf - ce) - q(af - cd) + r(ae - bd)\). Note the minus sign on the middle term.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The cross product of two vectors is a vector; the dot product is a scalar.
2. \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) is perpendicular to both \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\).
3. It is defined only for vectors in space.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Treating \(\times\) like ordinary multiplication: the order of the vectors changes the sign of the answer.
2. Writing the answer of a cross product as a number. \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) is a vector; only its magnitude \(|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}|\) is a number.
